newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Occidental's Colombian oil output falling.
newsitem.headline: Occidental's Colombian oil output falling.

text.p: U.S. oil company Occidental is still producing about 180,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil from its Colombian Cano Limon field after more than 10 years of exploitation, but output is set to decline over the next few years, company officials said on Tuesday.
Speaking at an energy conference here, Occidental Colombia president Stephen Newton said the company has produced 750 million out of Cano Limon's 1.1 billion barrels of reserves.
Output is expected to fall by about 10 percent per year until Occidental's licence runs out in 2007, when Newton said production would still be above 30,000 bpd.

Occidental was very interested in new exploration in Colombia, Newton added, but he joined voices with other conference delegates from some 50 U.S. energy companies in calling for better fiscal and contractual terms to encourage investment.

The Colombian government takes about 83 percent in taxes from oil projects, one of the highest levels in Latin America. Energy and Mines Minister Rodrigo Villamizar recognised that this was too high for new exploration projects where production costs were already high due to complicated geologial structures.
Delegates added that security measures alone could add another 10-15 percent to operating costs in Colombia.
Newton said the Cano Limon pipeline had been blown up 462 times since it started operation, a rate of about 45-50 times per year.
Indigenous rights and environmental matters were another key concern for the company, he added.

The 1991 constitution, although it had laudable objectives of protecting indigenous peoples' rights, had a negative effect on the oil industry because the enabling measures of the laws had not been passed.
"It puts companies and ministries in a difficult position... and affects every major infrastructure project in the country," he said.

Occidental recently won the right to explore for oil in northwest Colombia, home to the indigenous U'wa community who had previously obtained a high court ruling preventing any exploration on their territory.

"Hopefully we will now be able to persuade all the interested parties to sit down and discuss the rights of the Indians and also the rights of the other Colombians to develop the resources in their subsoil," Newton said.
He said Colombia had an admirable history of economic growth and that Colombia's independent judiciary was a major asset to the country.
